title: Liao-Fan's Four Instructions (Original Text)
excerpt: In my childhood I lost my father, and my old mother ordered me to abandon the pursuit of the examinations and study medicine, saying: "It can sustain one's life and aid others; and to master a skill and gain renown through it was your father's long-standing wish."

inline.s: In my childhood I lost my father, and my old mother ordered me to abandon the pursuit of the examinations and study medicine, saying: "It can sustain one's life and aid others; and to master a skill and gain renown through it was your father's long-standing wish."

Later, at Ciyun Temple, I met an old man with long whiskers and a noble bearing, graceful as an immortal, and I made him a respectful bow. He said to me, "You are one destined for the road of office; next year you will enter the school. Why do you not study?" I told him the reason, and asked his surname and dwelling. He said, "My surname is Kong, and I am a man of Yunnan. I have received the true transmission of Master Shao Yong's supreme principles of Number, and the appointment to pass the Number on belongs to you." I brought him home and told my mother, who said, "Treat him well."

I put his Number to the test, and every minutest detail proved true, whereupon I turned my mind to study. I consulted my cousin Shen Cheng, who said, "Mr. Yu Haigu is opening a school at the home of Shen Youfu. It will be most convenient for me to send you there to study." I accordingly took Yu as my teacher.

Kong cast the Number for me: in the county examination I should be ranked fourteenth among the candidates; in the prefectural examination seventy-first; in the educational commissioner's examination ninth. The following year I sat the examinations, and my ranks in the three places all matched.

He further divined the fortune and misfortune of my whole life, saying: "Such-and-such a year you will place such-and-such in the examination; such-and-such a year you will be made a stipendiary student; such-and-such a year you will be presented as tribute; after the tribute, such-and-such a year you will be appointed a magistrate of a county in Sichuan, and after three and a half years in office you should ask to return home. On the fourteenth day of the eighth month in your fifty-third year, at the hour of the ox, you shall end your days in your own bed, but alas without a son." I recorded it all and kept it carefully in mind.

From that time on, whenever I took examinations, the order of my ranks never deviated from what Mr. Kong had fixed. Only, in reckoning my stipend of rice, I had calculated that ninety-one dan and five dou would bring the tribute; yet after I had eaten somewhat over seventy dan, the commissioner Tu approved me for the tribute. I privately doubted this, and in the end it was rejected by the acting seal-holder, Mr. Yang.
Until the dingmao year (Master Liao-Fan's

nd year), the commissioner Yin Qiuming saw my reserve scroll in the examination hall and sighed, "These five policy essays — they are five memorials to the throne! How can so broad and penetrating a scholar be left to grow old beneath the window!" Whereupon, according to the county's submission, I was approved for the tribute; counting the rice I had already eaten, it was in truth ninety-one dan and five dou.

Because of this I believed all the more that "advance and retreat are decreed, and speed and delay have their seasons," and became calm, no longer seeking anything. Presented as tribute to the capital of Yan, I remained in the capital for a year, sitting in stillness all day and never opening a book.
In the jisi year I returned (Master Liao-Fan's

th year), and traveled to the Southern Academy. Before entering the academy I first visited Yungu, and met the Zen master among the Qixia mountains. We sat facing each other in a single room and did not close our eyes for some three days and nights. Yungu asked, "How is it that a man cannot become a sage? Only because he is bound by false thoughts. You have sat three days and I see you have not raised a single false thought — why is this?" I replied, "Mr. Kong has cast my whole fate. Honor and disgrace, life and death, are all fixed by Number. Even if I wished to be filled with false thoughts, I have nothing to be falsely thinking about."

Yungu laughed and said, "I took you for a hero; in truth you are only an ordinary man!" On being asked why, he said, "A man who cannot be without a mind is still bound by yin and yang — how could he be free of Number? But only ordinary men have a Number. The very best of men, Number cannot hold fast; the very worst of men, Number also cannot hold fast. For twenty years you have been held fast by his calculations, without turning a hair — is that not to be an ordinary man?"

I asked, "Then can Number be escaped?" He answered, "'Destiny is made by myself; fortune is sought in myself.' What the Book of Songs and the Book of History say is indeed a clear instruction. My own scriptures say: 'Seek wealth and honor, and you obtain wealth and honor; seek a son, and you obtain a son; seek long life, and you obtain long life.' Now, falsehood is a great precept of Sakyamuni — could the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas deceive men with lies?"

I pressed on, "Mencius says, 'Seek and you will obtain it — for this seeking is in my own power.' The virtues of morality and benevolence can be sought by effort; but how can merit, rank, wealth, and honor be sought for?" (Elaboration)

Yungu said, "Mencius's words are not wrong; it is your own understanding of them that is wrong. Do you not see what the Sixth Patriarch said? 'All fields of fortune lie no farther than this square inch of mind; seek from the mind, and there is no thought that does not reach.' If the seeking is in myself, then not only do I obtain the virtues of morality and benevolence, but I also obtain merit, rank, wealth, and honor — both within and without are obtained, and this is a seeking that profits in the obtaining. If instead one does not turn back and reflect within, but merely rushes outward in pursuit, then though the seeking has its way, the obtaining has its fate; both within and without are lost, and so there is no profit."

Then he asked, "What did Mr. Kong cast for your whole life?" I told him truthfully. Yungu said, "Do you yourself judge — ought you to obtain the examinations and rank? Ought you to have a son?" (Elaboration)

I reflected for a long time, then said, "I should not. Those in the ranks of the examinations generally have the appearance of good fortune. My fortune is thin, and I cannot accumulate merit and amass virtue to ground a deep fortune. Besides, I cannot bear the vexatious and busy, cannot tolerate others, and sometimes outshine men with my talent and cleverness, acting straight and speaking lightly. All these are marks of thin fortune — how could I be fit for the examinations!

The fouler the ground, the more living things it grows; the clearest water often has no fish. My love of cleanliness is the first reason I should have no son. Harmony can nurture the ten thousand things; my ready anger is the second reason I should have no son. Love is the root of generation; cruelty is the root of no generation. I cling to my reputation and often cannot set aside myself to save others — this is the third reason I should have no son. Much talking wastes the vital breath — the fourth reason. My fondness for drink wastes the essence — the fifth reason. I love to sit through the night in long meditation, and do not know how to treasure primal energy and nurture the spirit — the sixth reason. There are yet many other faults and evils, which I cannot enumerate fully."

Yungu said, "Not only the examinations! One in the world who enjoys an estate of a thousand gold pieces is surely a man of a thousand gold pieces; one who enjoys an estate of a hundred gold pieces is surely a man of a hundred gold pieces; one who is to die of hunger is surely a man who dies of hunger. Heaven does no more than apportion according to one's substance — has it ever added so much as a hair's breadth of intent?

Take the begetting of sons: one who has a hundred generations of virtue is sure to have descendants who preserve it for a hundred generations; one who has ten generations of virtue, descendants who preserve it for ten generations; one who has three or two generations of virtue, descendants who preserve it for three or two generations. And those who are cut off without posterity — their virtue is thinnest of all."

Now that you know your faults, do your utmost to wash away the conditions of your failure in the examinations and of your having no son: set your mind on accumulating virtue, on being tolerant of all, on harmony and love, and on treasuring your spirit. The past, in all its many kinds, is as though it died yesterday. The future, in all its many kinds, is as though it is born today — this is the body reborn of principle."

Now the body of flesh and blood still has its Number; how can the body of principle not move Heaven? Taijia said: 'The calamity Heaven brings may still be avoided; but the calamity one brings upon oneself cannot be lived through.' The Book of Songs says: 'Ever mindful of the decree, seek from yourself much fortune.' That Mr. Kong cast you as failing the examinations and having no son — this is the calamity Heaven brings, which may still be avoided. Now if you broaden your virtuous nature, diligently practice good deeds, and store up much hidden virtue, this is the fortune you yourself make — how can you fail to enjoy it?

The Changes counsels the gentleman to pursue good fortune and avoid misfortune. If the decree of Heaven were fixed and unchanging, how could good fortune be pursued, and how could misfortune be avoided? The very first principle of the opening chapter says: 'A household that accumulates goodness is sure to have an overflowing of blessing.' Can you be confident of this?"

I believed his words, bowed, and received his teaching. Thereupon I bared all the offenses of my past life before the Buddha, and wrote a petition, begging first for passing the examinations, and vowed to perform three thousand good deeds to requite the virtue of Heaven, Earth, and my ancestors.

Yungu produced a record of merits and demerits and showed it to me, ordering me to register each done deed day by day: good deeds were tallied, evil deeds were deducted. He also taught me to hold the mantra of Cundi, so that it would certainly be fulfilled.

He told me, "Among the masters of talismans there is a saying: 'One who cannot write a talisman is laughed at by gods and ghosts.' Here there is a secret transmission — it is simply not to stir the thought. When you take up the brush to write a talisman, first put down all the ten thousand ties, and not a single speck of dust arises. Then, from the place where the thought does not stir, set a single dot — this is called opening the foundation of primal chaos. From this, one stroke completes it, with no further deliberation, and the talisman is efficacious. All prayer to Heaven for the establishment of destiny must be felt through and reached in the place where there is no thought and no deliberation.

Mencius discoursed on the study of establishing destiny and said, 'Death and longevity are not held as two.' Now death and longevity are things held as utterly two! When the thought is not stirred, which is death and which is longevity? Dividing it finely: wealth and poverty not held as two, and then the destiny of rich and poor can be established; success and failure not held as two, and then the destiny of noble and base can be established; death and longevity not held as two, and then the destiny of life and death can be established. In a man's life in this world, death and life are the weightiest; speak of death and longevity, and all the smooth and the adverse are included within it."

As for 'cultivating the self to await it,' this is the matter of accumulating virtue and praying to Heaven. To say 'cultivate' means that whatever faults and evils the self has are all to be treated and done away with; to say 'await' means that the least covetous hope, the least anticipating welcome, are all to be cut off utterly. When one reaches this stage, one has gone straight into the state of the prior to Heaven — this is itself real learning!"

You are not yet able to be without a mind, but you can hold the mantra of Cundi. Count it without counting, without letting it be broken; when you hold it to full familiarity, then holding without holding, and in the not-holding, holding, until the thought does not stir — then it will be efficacious."
I had first taken the style name Xuehai; on that day I changed it to Liaofan, because I had awakened to the doctrine of establishing destiny and did not wish to fall into the rut of ordinary men.

From that time on, I was vigilant the whole day, and felt a difference from before. Formerly I had been aimless and self-indulgent; from then on there was naturally a scene of trembling watchfulness and alert dread. Even in a dark room or a leaky roof I was ever in fear of offending Heaven, Earth, and the gods and ghosts; and when men hated and slandered me, I was able to receive it calmly and with forbearance.

The next year, at the Ministry of Rites examination for the provincial degree, Mr. Kong had calculated I should place third; suddenly I placed first, and his word did not hold — and I passed in the autumn examination.

Yet my practice of righteousness was not pure, and my examination of myself had many errors. Sometimes I saw good and did not act on it bravely; sometimes I wanted to save others yet the mind doubted within; sometimes I forced myself to good and yet my mouth had faulty words; sometimes I was disciplined when sober and let myself go when drunk. Offenses offsetting merit, my days were spent in vain.
From the jisi year when I made my vow until the jimao year (Master Liao-Fan's

th year), more than ten years passed, and only then were the three thousand good deeds fulfilled. At the time I was just entering the pass with Li Jian'an, and had not yet been able to dedicate the merit; in the gengchen year (
th year), returning south, I at last invited the venerables Xingkong and Huikong to dedicate the merit in the Dongta meditation hall.
Thereupon I raised the vow to seek a son, and likewise promised to perform three thousand good deeds. In the xinsi year (

th year), a son was born, Tianqi. After each deed I performed, I immediately wrote it down with a note. Your mother could not write, so at each deed she would take a goose-quill tube and print a red circle on the calendar day. Sometimes she fed the poor, sometimes she bought living creatures to set free, and on a single day there were more than ten circles. By the eighth month of the guiwei year (
th year), the tally of three thousand was fulfilled. I again invited Xingkong and his fellows to dedicate the merit at our home.
On the thirteenth day of the ninth month I again raised the vow to seek success in the metropolitan examination, and promised to perform ten thousand good deeds. In the bingxu year (

st year) I passed, and was appointed magistrate of Baodi. I set up a blank ledger called "The Register of Governing the Mind." Rising early, I would take my seat in the court, and my family would hand the ledger to the gate-keeper to place on the table; whatever good or evil I had done, however minute, was recorded in full. At night I would set a table in the courtyard, after the manner of Zhao Yuedao, and burn incense to report to Heaven.

Seeing that I did few good deeds, your mother would knit her brows and say, "Before, when I was at home helping in the good deeds, the three thousand were completed. Now you have vowed ten thousand, and in the yamen there is nothing to do — when will it be fulfilled?" One night I chanced to dream of a divine being, and I told him how hard it was to complete my good deeds. The god said, "The single matter of lowering the grain levy will complete all ten thousand." The fields of Baodi had been at two fen three li seven hao per mu; I had arranged to reduce it to one fen four li six hao. Since this matter had indeed taken place, my heart was much startled and doubtful.

It happened that the Zen master Huanyu came from Mount Wutai, and I told him of my dream and asked whether the matter was to be trusted. The master said, "When a good heart is true and earnest, a single deed may stand for ten thousand good deeds — how much more when the whole county's levy is reduced, and ten thousand people receive its blessing!" I thereupon gave a donation from my official salary and asked him, on Mount Wutai, to feed ten thousand monks and dedicate the merit.
Mr. Kong had calculated that I should meet a calamity in my fifty-third year. I never prayed for long life, yet that year I passed through unharmed, and I am now sixty-nine.

The Book of History says, "Heaven is hard to trust; destiny is unchanging... rather, destiny is not constant." It also says, "Only destiny is not constant." These are no false words. From this I know that all that says fortune and misfortune are sought by oneself is the speech of the sages and the wise; while saying that fortune and misfortune are merely decreed by Heaven is the talk of the vulgar world.

Your destiny is not yet known. Even if destiny should make you honored and illustrious, always think of it as though you were fallen and alone; even if your course should be smooth, always think of it as though it were thwarted; even if you have abundant food before your eyes, always think of it as though you were poor and needy; even if men love and respect you, always think of it with fear; even if your family is of high repute, always think of yourself as lowly; even if your learning is quite excellent, always think of it as shallow and mean.

Think afar to glorify the virtue of your ancestors; think near to cover the faults of your parents. Think above to repay the grace of the state; think below to build the fortune of your family. Think outward to relieve men's emergencies; think inward to restrain your own evil.

Be sure each day to know your faults, and each day to reform them. One day without knowing a fault is one day of dwelling at ease in what you think is right; one day with no fault to correct is one day with no step forward. In the world there is no lack of bright and handsome people, and yet their virtue is not cultivated and their learning is not broadened — only because of two words, "going along," they waste a whole life.

The doctrine of establishing destiny imparted by Zen master Yungu is the finest, deepest, truest, and most correct of principles. Ruminate on it and strive to practice it, and do not let yourself be idle.

In the Spring and Autumn period, when the great officers saw a man's speech and movement, they would conjecture and speak of his fortune or misfortune, and there was scarcely one that did not come true, as may be seen in the records of the Zuo Commentary and the National Annals. In general, the omens of good and ill fortune arise in the mind and stir in the four limbs. Those who are over-generous in nature often obtain fortune; those who are over-thin in nature often draw near to calamity. The vulgar eye, much clouded, says that there are things unsettled and beyond foretelling. One who is utterly sincere and accords with Heaven — when fortune is about to come, look upon his goodness and you must know it beforehand; when calamity is about to come, look upon his not-goodness and you must know it beforehand.
Now, to obtain fortune and avoid calamity, one does not first speak of practicing good, but must first reform faults. But as to reforming faults:
First, one must arouse the mind of shame.
Think: the sages and worthies of old were men like me — how is it they can be teachers for a hundred generations, and I am broken like a tile in a single body?

Given over to worldly passions, privately practicing unrighteousness, thinking that others do not know, and proudly without shame — one will daily sink into being a beast without knowing it. Of what a man should be ashamed in this world, nothing is greater than this! Mencius says, "The sense of shame is great for a man." Because with it one becomes a sage; without it, a beast. This is the crucial moment of reforming faults.
Second, one must arouse the mind of fear.

Heaven and Earth are above, and the gods and ghosts are hard to deceive. Though my fault be hidden and minute, Heaven and Earth and the gods and ghosts truly oversee it. If heavy, they send down a hundred calamities; if light, they diminish one's present fortune. How can I not fear?

Not only this. In a place of idleness, the pointing and gazing are clear to all. Though I conceal it very closely and gloss it over very cleverly, my lungs and liver are already exposed, and in the end I cannot deceive myself; if a man sees through it, I am not worth a penny. How can I not tremble in awe?

Not only this. While a single breath remains, even the greatest evil that fills the sky can still be repented and reformed. Among the ancients there was one who did evil all his life, and at the point of death repented, aroused a single good thought, and so came to a good end — this is to say that a single fierce thought suffices to wash away a hundred years of evil. It is like a dark valley for a thousand years: at the first shining of a single lamp, the darkness of a thousand years is all removed. Hence faults are not to be regarded for age or youth, but only reformation is prized. But the dusty world is inconstant, the body of flesh is easily destroyed; once the breath is gone, there is no way to reform. In the open, one bears an evil name for a thousand autumns and a hundred generations, which even filial sons and kind grandsons cannot wash away; in the hidden, one sinks for a hundred ages in the retribution of the hells, which even sages, worthies, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot draw back. How can one not fear?
Third, one must arouse the mind of courage.

Men do not reform their faults mostly from going along and retreating. I must rouse myself and press on, without hesitation and without waiting. For the small, like a thorn in the flesh, quickly pull it out; for the great, like a poisonous snake biting the finger, quickly cut it away. Let there be not the slightest delay or hesitation — this is why the wind and thunder are of benefit.
With these three minds, then one reforms at every fault, like spring ice meeting the sun — how could one worry that it would not melt?
Yet men's faults are reformed sometimes from the matter, sometimes from the principle, sometimes from the mind; the effort is different, and the effect differs accordingly.

As when of old I killed living beings, and now I vow not to kill; of old I angered and cursed, and now I vow not to anger — this is reforming in respect of the matter itself. To restrain forcibly on the outside is a hundred times harder, and the root of the illness remains in the end; extinguishing in the east and arising in the west, it is not the way of ultimately open, vast clarity.

He who is good at reforming faults, before forbidding the matter, first clarifies its principle. If the fault lies in killing, straightway reflect: Heaven above loves life, and all creatures cling to life; to kill them to nourish myself — how can I be at ease? Moreover, when they are killed, first they suffer the knife and the cut, and then enter the cauldron and the boiling pan, with all kinds of pain piercing to the marrow of the bone. And for my nourishment rare delicacies are arrayed, and once eaten they come to nothing; plain food and simple broth suffice to fill the belly — why must I destroy their lives and diminish my own fortune?

Again think: all that have blood and vital breath contain spiritual awareness; since they have awareness, they are of one body with me. Even if I cannot cultivate to the highest virtue, to make them revere me and love me, how can I daily destroy their lives, making them my enemies and filling them with hatred of me without end? At the first thought of this, there will be times when, facing food, the heart is grieved and the throat cannot swallow.

As of old I was given to anger — I must reflect: when a man falls short, it is a matter that calls for compassion; when he offends contrary to principle, what is it to me? There is essentially nothing to be angry at. Again think: in the world there is no hero who holds himself always right, and no learning that blames others. When conduct does not attain, it is all because my own virtue is not cultivated and my influence has not reached. If I turn it wholly back upon myself, then the coming of slander and blame is the place that has ground and polished me into completion; I will joyfully receive the gift — what is there to be angry at? Again, to hear slander and not be angry, though the blaze of calumny smoke the very heavens, is like lifting a torch to burn the sky, which in the end will go out by itself. To hear slander and be angry, though one craftily marshal a defense, is like the spring silkworm making its cocoon, bringing entanglement upon itself. Anger is not only without benefit, it is positively harmful.
For all the other kinds of faults and evils, one should likewise reflect upon them by principle. Once this principle is clear, the fault will stop of itself.

What is meant by reforming from the mind? Faults have a thousand ends, and are all made by the mind. If my mind does not stir, from what can the fault arise? Among students, in the various faults of lust for beauty, lust for fame, lust for goods, lust for anger, one need not seek them out one by one by category; one has only to be single-minded in goodness and the right thought to appear before the mind, and the evil thought will of itself not defile it. It is like the sun hanging in the sky, while the goblins and specters vanish on their own — this is the true transmission of the single and the undivided! Faults are made by the mind, and also reformed by the mind; as in cutting down a poisonous tree, cut straight through its root — why must one fell branch by branch and pluck leaf by leaf?

Generally, the very highest governs the mind, and is pure at once; the moment it stirs one is aware, and being aware it is gone. If one cannot yet do this, one must clarify the principle to dismiss it; if one cannot yet do that, one must follow the matter to forbid it. To take up the higher work while also practicing the lower effort is no wrong move; but to cling to the lower and be blind to the higher is clumsy.

Now, when one vows to reform faults, in the open he needs good friends to remind him, and in the hidden he needs gods and ghosts to bear witness; with single-minded repentance, unremitting by day and night, passing through one week of seven, then two weeks, even to a month, two months, three months, there must be an effect. You may feel the mind-spirit serene and broad; or feel wisdom suddenly opened; or amid the lingering and the muddled, every thought one touches goes through; or meet an enemy and turn anger into joy; or dream of vomiting black things; or dream of past sages and worthies taking you by the hand and leading you; or dream of flying astride the great void; or dream of banners and jeweled canopies. Such excellent matters are all the signs of faults dissolved and offenses extinguished.

Yet one must not seize on these and think himself high, drawing a line and not advancing. Of old, Qu Boyu at twenty had already felt the faults of the days before and reformed them all; at twenty-one he knew that what he had reformed before was not yet complete; and at twenty-two, looking back on twenty-one, was still as though in a dream. Year after year he reformed them in succession, and arriving at fifty he still knew the faults of his forty-nine years. Such was this ancient's study of reforming faults! We who are but this generation's ordinary run, with faults gathered thick as thorns; yet looking back on past affairs, often appear not to see our faults — the mind is coarse and the eye is clouded.

But for those whose faults and sins are deep and heavy, there are also such signs: the mind-spirit is darkened and blocked, and turning the head one forgets; or with nothing to do one is ever troubled; or meeting a gentleman one blushes and is cast down; or hearing right discourse one is not pleased; or one bestows kindness and men instead resent it; or at night one dreams in confusion, and worse, speaks wildly and loses his bearing. All these are marks of making offenses. If one is like any of these, one must rouse up, abandon the old and seek the new, and be sure not to ruin himself!

The Changes says, "A household that accumulates goodness is sure to have an overflowing of blessing." Of old, when the Yan family was to give its daughter in marriage to Shulianghe, it set forth in order the long accumulation of virtue by his ancestors, and foreknew that his descendants would surely have those who would arise. Confucius praised Shun's great filiality, saying, "The ancestral temple offered to him, and descendants preserved it." These are all the highest discourses; let us test them by past events:

The junior grand secretary Yang Rong was a man of Jianning, whose family for generations made a living by ferrying people across. After long rains the streams swelled, and the flooding waters swept away the people's dwellings, with the drowned floating down on the current. The other boats all gathered up the goods, but Rong's great-grandfather and grandfather alone saved the people, taking nothing of the goods, while the villagers laughed at them as fools. By the time Rong's father was born, the family had gradually grown well-off. A divine being appeared disguised as a Taoist and said to him, "Your grandfather and great-grandfather had hidden merit; their descendants should be honored and illustrious, and you should bury them at such-and-such a place." So they followed his pointing and buried them there — this is the present White Rabbit grave. Afterward Rong was born, passed the examinations while still young, and rose to the rank of the Three Dukes, with his great-grandfather, grandfather, and father given the same offices. His descendants flourished in honor, and to this day there are many worthy ones among them.

Yang Zicheng of Yin county was at first a county clerk, with a kind and generous heart, and he upheld the law with fairness. At that time the county magistrate was stern, and on one occasion beat a prisoner until the blood flowed before him, yet his anger was not appeased; Yang knelt and eased his mind. The magistrate said, "What can I do? This man has overstepped the law and violated principle, so of course there is no keeping from anger." Zicheng kowtowed and said, "When those above have lost the Way, the people have long been scattered. If one obtains the truth of the case, one should have compassion and not be glad; to be glad is not even acceptable — how much more to be angry?" The magistrate was soothed into a smiling face. His family was very poor, and he took nothing of the gifts offered; when prisoners lacked food, he would often help them by every means.

One day there were several newly imprisoned men awaiting food, and his family had run short of grain. To feed the prisoners, his family would go without; to look to his own, the prisoners were pitiable. He consulted his wife, who said, "Where do the prisoners come from?" He said, "They come from Hangzhou. Along the way they endured hunger, and the green of famine is plain upon their faces." So he took his own rice and cooked gruel to feed the prisoners.

Afterward two sons were born to him, the elder named Shouchen and the younger Shouzhi, who both became vice ministers of the Ministry of Rites for the south and north; his eldest grandson was a vice minister of Justice, and his second grandson a provincial judge in Sichuan. All became famous ministers, and today Chuting and Dezheng are also of his line.

During the Zhengtong era, Deng Maoqi raised rebellion in Fujian, and very many scholars and commoners followed the bandits. The court raised the censors-in-chief Zhang Kai of Yin county to campaign south, and he captured the bandits by stratagem. Afterwards the matter was entrusted to the commissioner Xie Dushi, who searched out and killed the bandit partisans on the eastern road. Xie sought the register of those who had joined the bandits' party, and to all who had not joined them he secretly gave small white cloth flags, arranging that when the troops arrived they should plant the flags at their gates, and he warned the soldiers not to kill recklessly, so that ten thousand lives were spared. Later Xie's son Qian won the rank of zhuangyuan and became a grand minister; his grandson Pi likewise was again among the top three.

The Lin family of Putian: an old mother of an earlier generation was fond of goodness, and would always make rice-flour balls to give to others, giving them to whoever asked without ever tiring. An immortal, transformed as a Taoist, would come each morning to ask for six or seven balls, and the mother gave them day after day, three full years as one day, and only then did he know her sincerity. So he said to her, "I have eaten your rice-flour balls for three years — how shall I repay you? Behind your house there is a plot of ground; if you bury there, your descendants will have offices and rank in a count of a liter of sesame seeds." Her son buried her as he had pointed out, and in the very first generation nine gained the examination rank; generation after generation the caps and tassels were very many, and in Fujian there ran the saying, "No Lin, no opening of the examination roll."

The father of the historiographer Feng Zhuoan was a student in the county school. Rising early on a bitter winter morning and going to school, he met a man lying fallen in the snow and felt of him; he was half-rigid. So he took off his own padded jacket and covered him, and also carried him home and revived him. He dreamed that a god told him, "You saved a man's life, out of a most sincere heart; I am sending Han Qi to be your son." When Zhuoan was born, he was accordingly named Qi.

The minister Ying of Taizhou studied at the mountain in his prime. The ghosts at night would gather and shriek, often startling people, but the master was unafraid. One night he heard a ghost say, "A certain woman, because her husband has long been away and not returned, is being pressed by her parents-in-law to marry another; tomorrow night she will hang herself here, and I shall get a successor." The master secretly sold land for four taels of silver, wrote a letter in counterfeit of the husband's hand, and sent the silver home. When the parents saw the letter, they were suspicious that the handwriting was unlike his; then they said, "The letter may be a forgery, but the silver cannot be false; the boy must be well." So the woman did not remarry. Her son in the end returned, and husband and wife were preserved to each other as before.

The master again heard the ghost say, "I was to have my successor, but this xiucai has spoiled my affair." Beside him another ghost said, "Why do you not bring calamity on him?" He replied, "Heaven, because this man's heart is good, has appointed him a minister of hidden virtue. How can I bring calamity on him?" Because of this Ying was all the more spurred on, adding to his goodness day by day and deepening his virtue day by day. In years of famine he would donate grain to relieve; when his relatives had urgent need he would bend over backward to sustain them; and when faced with violence and wrong he would turn back upon himself and blame himself, accepting it with calm. His descendants who gained the examination rank are, to this day, many.

Xu Fengzhu, styled Zhi, of Changshu, had a father who was well-off. Once when a year of famine chanced, he first donated his rent as a lead for the same county, and then divided grain to relieve the poor and needy. At night he heard ghosts singing at his gate: "A thousand no lie, ten thousand no lie, the Xu family's xiucai is made a juren." Calling in succession, without a break all night; that year Fengzhu indeed passed in the provincial examination. His father therefore accumulated virtue all the more, spiriting without rest; he built bridges and repaired roads, fed monks and received the people, and whatever could benefit, he did with all his heart. Later he heard ghosts again singing at the gate: "A thousand no lie, ten thousand no lie, the Xu family's juren goes straight on to the High Court." Fengzhu's office ended as the governor of the two Zhe regions.

Master Tu Kangxi of Jiaxing first was a principal secretary in the Ministry of Justice; lodging in the prison, he carefully questioned the conditions of the various prisoners and obtained a number of the innocent. The master did not take it as his own achievement, but secretly noted the business and laid it before the high officials. Later at the autumn assizes, the high officials picked out his words to interrogate the various prisoners, and there was none who did not submit; more than ten were released from wrongful imprisonment. For a time the whole capital praised the minister's clarity.

The master further stated, "Beneath the very wheels of the capital there are still many wronged people; across the wide four seas, among the myriad numbered people, how can there be no innocent? One should every five years send a commissioner of the reduction of punishment, to verify and set right." The minister memorialized it, and the proposal was approved; at the time, the master was one of those sent to reduce the sentences. He dreamed a god told him, "Your fate is to have no son. Now this proposal of reducing punishment closely accords with the mind of Heaven, and Heaven grants you three sons, all robed in purple and girt with gold." That very night his lady conceived, and afterward bore Yingxun, Yingkun, and Yingling, all of whom became distinguished officials.

Bao Ping of Jiaxing, styled Xinzhi, had a father who was the magistrate of Chiyang. Of seven sons Bao Ping was the youngest, and he was taken as a son-in-law into the Yuan family of Pinghu, with whom my father had close relations. Broad in learning and of high talent, he sat the examinations again and again without passing, and gave his mind to the learning of the two schools. One day, traveling east to the Mao lake, he chanced on a village temple and saw an image of Avalokiteshvara dripping wet and standing in the open, so he straightway untied his purse, found ten taels of silver, and gave them to the abbot to repair the hall. The monk told him the work was great and the silver little, and it could not be completed. He took out four bolts of loose silk and, searching his bag, gave seven garments besides; among them a hempen folded robe was newly made, and his servant begged him to keep it. Ping said, "If only the holy image be safe, what harm though I be stripped bare?" The monk shed tears and said, "To give silver, garments, and silk is not hard; but this single heart of yours — how hard to come by!" After the work was done, he brought his old father along to visit and lodged in the temple. The master dreamed that the guardian deity came to thank him, saying, "Your son shall enjoy a hereditary stipend." Later his son Bian and grandson Zhifang both passed the examinations and became distinguished officials.

The father of Zhi Li of Jiashan was a clerk in the penal office. There was a prisoner wrongly caught in a grave capital charge, and he was moved to pity and sought to save the man's life. The prisoner said to his wife, "Mr. Zhi has kindness in his heart, but I grieve that I have nothing to repay him with. Tomorrow invite him down into the countryside, and you offer your body to him; if he is perhaps willing to use his mind on it, then I may live." His wife wept and obeyed the command. When he arrived, the wife came out to press wine and told him plainly her husband's intention. Zhi would not listen, and in the end did his utmost to have the case reversed.

When the prisoner came out of prison, husband and wife came to the door to kowtow in thanks, saying, "The master's virtue is so thick that it is rare in these later days. Now, having no son, we have a young daughter, and we give her to be your humble maid — this is a matter the rites permit." Zhi prepared the gifts and took her in, and she bore Li, who passed the examination while young and rose to the office of a secretary duplicator in the Hanlin Academy. Li bore Gao, and Gao bore Lu, both of whom were presented as tribute and became instructors in the school; Lu bore Dalun, who passed the examination.

These ten cases all practiced differently, yet all returned to goodness. If we further speak precisely, then good has the true and the false, the upright and the crooked, the hidden and the open, the right and the wrong, the partial and the complete, the half and the full, the great and the small, the difficult and the easy — all of these must be carefully distinguished. To do good without exhausting the principle, one thinks one is practicing the holding, yet one is making offenses; to vex one's heart in vain is of no benefit.
What are the true and the false?

Of old, several Confucian students went to visit the monk Zhongfeng, and said, "The Buddhists treat good and evil and their retribution as shadow following form. Now this man is good, yet his descendants do not prosper; that man is evil, yet his household flourishes — the Buddha's words have no basis!" Zhongfeng said, "Worldly feelings not yet washed away, the right eye not yet opened, acknowledging good as evil and pointing to evil as good — this often happens. Should you not grieve that your own right and wrong are inverted, but instead resent that Heaven's retribution falls short?" The assembly said, "How do good and evil come to be the reverse?" Zhongfeng bade them try to describe it. One said, "To curse men and beat men is evil; to revere men and be courteous to men is good." Zhongfeng said, "That is not necessarily so." Another said, "To greedily grasp wealth and take it wrongly is evil; to be incorruptible and keep to right is good." Zhongfeng said, "That is not necessarily so."

The whole company detailed their descriptions, and Zhongfeng said none of them were so. So they asked, and Zhongfeng told them, "What benefits others is good; what benefits oneself is evil. If it benefits others, then beating men and cursing men are good; if it benefits oneself, then revering men and being courteous to men are evil. Therefore, in a man's doing good, what benefits others is public, and being public it is true; what benefits oneself is private, and being private it is false. Again, what roots in the heart is true; what imitates the traces is false. Again, the good done without deliberate doing is true; the good done with deliberate doing is false. All of these are to be examined by oneself."
What are the upright and the crooked?

People today, seeing a cautious, agreeable man, call him good and take to him by kind; the sage, however, would rather take the wild and the self-possessed (kuang and juan). As for the cautious, agreeable man, though a whole village likes him, yet he must be regarded as the thief of virtue — such is the world's good and evil, directly opposite to the sage. Push this one point, and in all the many taking and rejecting there is none that is not mistaken; Heaven, Earth, and the gods and ghosts, in rewarding the good and afflicting the licentious, all share the sage's right and wrong, and do not share the world's taking and rejecting. Whoever wants to accumulate good absolutely must not follow the ear and eye, but only, from the hidden and minute place of the mind's source, silently wash clean. If it is purely a heart of saving the world, it is upright; if there is the least heart of currying favor with the world, it is crooked. If it is purely a heart of loving others, it is upright; if there is the least heart of anger at the world, it is crooked. If it is purely a heart of revering others, it is upright; if there is the least heart of playing with the world, it is crooked. All are to be carefully distinguished.
What are the hidden and the open?

When good is done where the world can see it, it is called open good (yang shan); when good is done where no one else knows, it is called hidden virtue (yin de). Hidden virtue is repaid by Heaven; open good earns worldly fame, and fame is itself a blessing. Yet fame is precisely what the Creator most resents. Those who enjoy great renown without truly deserving it are often overtaken by strange calamities, while those who, blameless themselves, are wrongly burdened with an ill name usually find their descendants suddenly flourishing. O how subtle is the line between the open and the hidden!
What is meant by “right” and “wrong”?

Under the laws of the State of Lu, any man of Lu who ransomed a countryman from servitude among the feudal lords was rewarded with gold from the state treasury. When Zi Gong ransomed a man but refused the gold, Confucius heard of it and disapproved, saying: “Ci has erred! When a sage undertakes a deed, he does so in order to change manners and correct customs, so that his teaching may be practiced by all the people — never merely to suit his own conduct. Now in Lu the rich are few and the poor are many. If accepting the reward is counted as base, how will there be any ransoming of one another from now on? From this day forth, no one will redeem the enslaved from the lords!”
When Zi Lu rescued a man from drowning, the man thanked him with an ox, and Zi Lu accepted it. Confucius was pleased and said: “From now on, there will be many in Lu who rescue people from drowning!”

Viewed through the common eye, Zi Gong’s refusal of the gold was superior and Zi Lu’s acceptance of the ox was inferior; yet Confucius favored Zi Lu and dismissed Zi Gong. From this we learn that in judging a man’s goodness we look not to the act alone but to its consequences; not to the passing moment but to the far future; not to one man but to the whole world. An act that is itself good, but whose consequences harm people, seems good yet is truly not; an act that is itself not good, but whose consequences benefit people, seems not good yet is truly so. Still, this is to judge only a single case. Other things — the righteousness that is not righteous, the propriety that is not proper, the trust that is not trustworthy, the kindness that is not kind — must all be carefully weighed.
What is meant by “deviant” and “upright”?

Long ago, when Lord Lü Wenyi first resigned his post as prime minister and returned to his native place, the whole realm looked up to him as one looks to Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper. A certain townsman, drunk, cursed him to his face. Lord Lü was unmoved and told his servant: “Do not argue with a drunkard; close the gate and ignore him.” A year later the man committed a capital crime and was thrown into prison. Only then did Lord Lü regret his leniency. “Had I pressed the matter at the time,” he said, “and had him dealt with by the authorities, a small punishment would have taught him a great lesson. I only wished to keep my heart generous and kind, and never thought I was fostering his wickedness until it came to this!” This is an instance of doing an evil deed with a good heart.

There are also those who do a good deed with an unkind heart. Suppose a wealthy household, in a year of famine, sees the poor openly pillaging grain from the market in broad daylight. When the matter is reported to the magistrate, the magistrate does nothing, and the poor grow only more brazen. At last the household seizes them and humiliates them, and only then do the crowds settle down — otherwise a riot would all but have broken out.

Thus the good is upright and the evil is deviant — this everyone knows. But one who does an evil deed with a good heart is upright yet slanted; one who does a good deed with an unkind heart is deviant yet upright. Of this one must not be ignorant.
What is meant by “half” and “full”?

The Book of Changes says: “If goodness is not accumulated, it is not enough to establish a name; if evil is not accumulated, it is not enough to destroy one’s life.” The Book of History says: “The crimes of Shang are full, even overflowing.” It is like storing things in a vessel: if you pile them up diligently, it overflows; if you are lax and do not pile them, it never fills. That is one view.

Long ago a certain woman entered a monastery wishing to make an offering but had no money — only two coppers, which she gave. The abbot himself performed the rites of confession for her. Later she entered the palace and grew rich, and carrying several thousand pieces of gold back to the monastery she made an offering. This time the abbot merely had his disciple recite the dedication. She asked: “When I first offered two coppers, Master performed the rites himself; now that I offer thousands, Master does not even recite the dedication. Why?” He replied: “Before, though the gift was slight, the giving heart was perfectly sincere, and had I not officiated myself it would not have answered your virtue. Now the gift is lavish, but the giving heart is not as earnest as it was before; it is enough that another performs the rites for you.” Thus those thousand pieces of gold were but half-good, while the two coppers were full-good.

Zhongli imparted the elixir to Patriarch Lü, teaching him to turn iron into gold that could relieve the world. Lü asked: “Will it ever turn back?” Zhongli answered: “After five hundred years it will return to its true substance.” Lü said: “Then I would be harming the people of five hundred years hence. I do not wish to do it.” Zhongli replied: “To cultivate the immortal path one must accumulate three thousand meritorious deeds; with this single word, your three thousand are already fulfilled.” This is yet another view.

Furthermore, in doing good, if the heart does not dwell upon the good, then whatever you accomplish will be complete and perfect; but if the heart clings to the good, though you strive diligently all your life, you will reach at most half-good. For instance, when one relieves others with wealth, not seeing oneself within, not seeing others without, not seeing the thing given in the middle — this is called the empty arising of the three wheels, the single heart made pure. Then a single peck of millet can plant blessings without bound, and a single coin can wash away the guilt of a thousand aeons. But if this heart is not yet forgotten, then even ten thousand catties of gold will not make the merit full. This is yet another view.
What is meant by “great” and “small”?

Long ago Wei Zhongda, holding office at the academy, was summoned to the underworld, where the ruler commanded a clerk to bring the two registers of his good and his evil. When they arrived, the register of evil filled the whole courtyard, while the register of good was a single scroll no thicker than a chopstick. When they were set on the scale, the one that filled the courtyard proved the lighter, and the single scroll proved the heavier. Zhongda asked: “I am not yet forty — how can my transgressions be so many?” The clerk answered: “A single unrighteous thought already counts; one need not have committed the deed.” Zhongda then asked what was written in the scroll. “On an occasion when the court undertook a great work and built the stone bridge over the Three Hills,” the clerk said, “you submitted a memorial urging against it; this is that draft.” Zhongda said: “Though I spoke, the court did not follow, and my words availed nothing — how can it carry such weight?” The clerk said: “Though the court did not follow, your single thought was already on behalf of the ten thousand people. Had they heeded you, the power of the good would have been even greater.” Wherefore, if your aim is the realm and its people, then though your good be small it is great; if your aim is only yourself, then though it be much, it is small.
What is meant by “difficult” and “easy”?

The scholars of old said: “In mastering self, one must begin where mastery is hardest.” The Master, speaking of practicing humaneness, likewise said: “In this, count the difficulties first.” Just so, the Old Man Shu of Jiangxi gave up the two years’ meager tuition he had barely earned to repay another’s official debt, and in doing so kept a husband and wife whole; and the Old Man Zhang of Handan gave up the money he had saved over ten years to make good a ransom, and in doing so preserved the lives of a man’s wife and children. Both are cases of being able to let go where it is hardest to let go.

Or the Old Man Jin of Zhenjiang, who though old and without a son could not bear to take a young girl as a concubine and sent her back to her neighbor — this is being able to forbear where it is hardest to forbear.

Therefore the blessings Heaven bestows upon them are deep as well. All who possess wealth and power find it easy to establish virtue; yet to have it easy and not do it is to abandon oneself. The poor and lowly find doing good difficult, but to do it when it is difficult — that alone is worthy of praise.

In following circumstances to help the multitude, the kinds of good are exceedingly numerous. To state their outline in brief, there are about ten: First, helping others toward the good; second, keeping love and respect in the heart; third, completing the good of others; fourth, urging others on to good; fifth, rescuing people in peril; sixth, building up great benefits; seventh, giving wealth to create blessings; eighth, upholding the true Dharma; ninth, honoring elders and superiors; tenth, cherishing the lives of all beings.
What is meant by “helping others toward the good”?

Long ago, when Shun was at Lei Ze, he saw that the fishermen all took the deep pools and the rich waters, while the old and weak fished only in the swift shallows. His heart ached with pity, and he went himself to fish. Whenever he saw men contending, he hid their faults without a word; whenever he saw one yielding to another, he praised it and made it his own model. Within a year, all were giving up the deep pools and the rich waters to one another. With Shun’s clear wisdom, could he not have spoken a single word to instruct the crowd? Yet he did not teach by words but turned them by his own example — this is the painstaking heart of a true craftsman!

We who live in this latter age must not use our own strengths to overshadow others, not use our own goodness to set others in a bad light, not use our own abilities to embarrass others. Gather in your talents and wisdom, being as though you had none, as though you were empty. When you see a fault in others, rather be lenient and cover it over — on the one hand to let them correct it, on the other that they may have some restraint and not dare run loose. When you see in anyone some small excellence worth taking up or some small good worth recording, turn about, let go of your own way, and follow theirs — and praise it warmly and speak of it widely. In all daily dealings, whether you utter a word or perform a deed, do not start from thought of yourself but always to set a standard for all beings; this is the measure of the great person who holds the world as the common good.
What is meant by “keeping love and respect in the heart”?

The gentleman and the petty man, viewed by their outward traces, are often hard to tell apart; but in that one point where the heart is set, good and evil stand utterly apart, as clearly opposed as black and white. Hence it is said: “What distinguishes the gentleman from other men is the way he holds his heart.” The heart a gentleman keeps is only a heart of love and a heart of respect. For among people there are near and far, noble and base, wise and foolish, worthy and unworthy; the ten thousand kinds are not one, yet all are our kin, all are one body with us — and who among them is not to be loved and respected? To love and respect the multitude is to love and respect the sages; to be able to reach the aims of the multitude is to reach the aims of the sages. Why? Because the aim of the sages is simply that this age and its people should each find their proper place. When I unite love and respect to bring peace to all the people of an age, I am bringing them peace on the sages’ behalf.
What is meant by “completing the good of others”?

Jade within the stone, cast aside, is but a shard and a pebble; when carved and polished, it becomes a jade scepter. So whenever you see a man do a good deed, or see in him a worthy aim and a talent that may be advanced, you must guide and support him toward his accomplishment. Either commend and encourage him, or keep him steady from behind, or clear the false charges against him and share in his blame — you must not rest until he has stood on his own. For the most part each man dislikes those not of his own kind; in a village the good are few and the not-good are many, so a good man among the vulgar finds it hard to stand alone. Moreover, the heroic and the outstanding pay little heed to the polish of outward traces and are so much the more easily blamed. Thus good causes often come to ruin and good men often meet with slander; only the humane and the elder, who set them straight and lend them support, gain the greatest merit of all.
What is meant by “urging others on to good”?

Born as human beings, who has no conscience? Yet on the weary road of the world one is most easily drowned and lost. Whenever you are with others, you should take occasion to rouse them and open their delusions — as one who wakes another from a deep dream of the long night, as one who draws a soul long sunk in affliction up into coolness and ease. Among benefits, this reaches farthest and widest. Han Yu said: “For a single lifetime one exhorts by speech; for a hundred generations one exhorts by books.” Compared with helping others toward the good, this has its outward traces, yet as a remedy fitted to the disease it works wonders and cannot be set aside. If you waste words on the wrong man, or pass by the right one, you must turn and reflect on your own wisdom.
What is meant by “rescuing people in peril”?

Hardship and calamity fall to everyone from time to time; when you chance upon such a case, you should feel it as a sore upon your own body and quickly come to its relief. Either by a single word you may right their wrongs and waylay their grievances, or by many means you may aid their distress. Master Cui said: “Kindness lies not in its greatness, but in hastening to another’s need.” Truly this is the word of a humane man!
What is meant by “building up great benefits”?

In a small matter within a single township, in a great matter within a whole district, whatever is of benefit ought especially to be built up. Either dig canals to guide the water, or build dikes to guard against harm, or repair bridges to ease the traveler, or give tea and food to relieve the hungry and thirsty. As occasions arise, persuade others and join forces to build; do not avoid suspicion, do not decline toil and blame.
What is meant by “giving wealth to create blessings”?

In the Buddhist path, of the ten thousand practices, giving comes first. What is called giving is nothing but the one word “relinquish.” The enlightened relinquish within the six sense organs, without the six sense objects, and all that they possess, so that nothing is withheld. If one cannot yet do this, begin by giving wealth. The world counts clothes and food as life itself, and so wealth is of the greatest weight. If we give it up, within we break through our own stinginess, and without we relieve the pressing need of others. At first it is strained; in the end it is calm and at ease. Nothing so thoroughly washes away selfish feeling and sweeps away clinging and miserliness.
What is meant by “upholding the true Dharma”?

The Dharma is the eye of sentient beings for ten thousand ages. Without the true Dharma, how could we join in fostering Heaven and Earth? How could we shape and complete the ten thousand things? How could we escape the dust and be freed from bondage? How could we manage the affairs of the world and yet go beyond the world? Therefore, whenever you see the shrines and images of the sages and the scriptures and books, you should hold them in reverence and keep them in repair. As for raising high the true Dharma and repaying the Buddha’s kindness above, this especially must be pursued with diligence.
What is meant by “honoring elders and superiors”?

The fathers and elder brothers of a family, the rulers of a state, and all those advanced in years, in virtue, in rank, or in insight, should be served with special care. At home, in serving your parents with deep love, a gentle countenance, a soft voice, and a lowered spirit, until it becomes second nature, you lay the very root of the harmony that moves Heaven. When you go forth to serve the sovereign, in doing a deed do not suppose the sovereign will not know and so give yourself free rein; in punishing a man do not suppose the sovereign will not know and so make a show of your authority. “To serve the sovereign as one serves Heaven” is a maxim of the ancients, and in such matters hidden virtue is most at stake. Look at the families of the loyal and the filial — their descendants never fail to be long-enduring and flourishing. Be very careful in this.
What is meant by “cherishing the lives of all beings”?

What makes a human being human is nothing but this heart of compassion — the pity and grief one feels at another’s suffering. The one who seeks humaneness seeks this; the one who accumulates virtue accumulates this. The Rites of Zhou says, “In the first month of spring, let no barren she-beast be used in sacrifice,” and Mencius says, “The gentleman keeps his distance from the kitchen” — all in order to preserve this heart of compassion. Hence the elders of old set forth the precept of the four not-eaten: not to eat what was killed within one’s hearing, not to eat what was killed within one’s sight, not to eat what one has raised oneself, and not to eat what was killed expressly for oneself.

Those who cannot yet give up meat should at least begin by observing these precepts. Advancing gradually, the compassionate heart grows all the while: not only killing must be guarded against, but every moving thing and every being with spirit is a life. In reeling silk one boils the cocoon, and in hoeing the field one takes the lives of insects. Reflect that food and clothing are all obtained by killing these others to keep ourselves alive, and so the guilt of wasting and destroying is no less than that of killing. As for what the hand wounds by mistake or the foot treads upon by error — who can reckon how often, and yet in every case one should take the utmost care to guard against it. An ancient poem says: “In love for the rats one always leaves them rice; in pity for the moths one lights no lamp.” How humane!
Good deeds are without limit and cannot be told to the full; but by taking these ten matters and extending them abroad, all the ten thousand virtues may be made complete!

The Book of Changes says: “The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and increases the humble; the Way of Earth transforms the full and pours it toward the humble; the spirits and gods harm the full and bless the humble; the way of man dislikes the full and is drawn to the humble.” Therefore the single hexagram of humility holds good fortune in all six lines. And the Book of History says: “Complacency brings loss; humility gains benefit.”

Often have I sat the examinations together with various gentlemen, and whenever I saw a poor scholar about to succeed, there was always a certain radiance of modesty about him that one could almost cup in the hands.
In the year Xinwei (

years of age), when I went up with the candidates to the capital, there were ten of my fellow townsmen from Jiashan in all, and only Ding Jingyu, who was the youngest, was exceedingly humble. I said to Fei Jinpo: “This friend will surely pass this year.” Fei asked: “How can you tell?” I replied: “Only humility receives blessing. Look among the ten — is there one so gentle and sincere, so unwilling to take precedence over others, as Jingyu? Is there one so respectful and deferential, so careful and humble, as Jingyu? Is there one who, insulted, makes no reply, and when slandered, does not dispute, as Jingyu? If a man can be like this, even Heaven and Earth and the spirits and gods will assist him — how could he fail to pass?” When the list was opened, Ding was indeed among the successful.
In the year Dingchou (

years of age), while I was in the capital I shared lodgings with Feng Kaizhi and saw how he had emptied himself and composed his bearing, greatly changed from the habits of his youth. Li Jiyan, a straightforward and honest friend, would often attack his faults to his face, yet every time one saw only an even heart and a compliant acceptance — never a single word in return. I told him: “Happiness has its beginnings and misfortune its forewarnings. If this heart is truly humble, Heaven will surely assist it. This year, my friend, you will certainly pass.” And it proved so.

Zhao Yufeng, named Guangyuan, a man of Guan County in Shandong, had won the provincial degree in his boyhood but for many years failed to pass the higher examination. His father served as third magistrate of Jiashan, and Yufeng accompanied him to his post. Admiring Qian Mingwu, he took his essay to show him. Mingwu struck out his essay entirely; Zhao not only did not grow angry but was convinced at heart and quickly corrected it. The next year he passed and obtained the degree.
In the year Renchen (

years of age), I went to the capital for an audience and there met Xia Jiansuo. I saw that his spirit was low and his bearing humble, and a modesty shone out from him. When I came home I told a friend: “Whenever Heaven is about to bring forth a man, before it reveals his good fortune it first reveals his wisdom; and once this wisdom is revealed, the shallow naturally become full and the unrestrained naturally draw in. Jiansuo is so gentle and good as this — Heaven has awakened him.” When the list was opened, he had indeed passed.
Zhang Weiyan of Jiangyin, a man of deep learning and accomplished writing, had a name in the literary world. In the year Jiawu (at Master Liaofan’s

years of age), when the provincial examination was held at Nanjing, he lodged in a certain temple. When the results were announced and his name was not among them, he cursed the examiners at length for being blindfolded. At that a certain Daoist beside him smiled, and Zhang at once turned his anger upon the Daoist. The Daoist said: “Sir, your essay assuredly was not good.” Zhang grew even angrier: “You have not seen my essay — how do you know it was not good?” The Daoist said: “I have heard that in writing essays the thing prized is a calm and even heart. Now to hear you cursing and reviling, your heart is far from even — how could the essay be fine?” Zhang could not help but yield, and so drew near to ask his guidance.

The Daoist said: “Passing the examination is entirely a matter of destiny; if destiny does not grant it, however fine the essay, it is of no use. But you must yourself make a turning.” Zhang said: “If it is destiny, how can it be turned?” The Daoist said: “What forges destiny is Heaven; what establishes destiny is myself. Devote yourself to good deeds and widely accumulate hidden virtue — what good fortune is there that cannot be sought?” Zhang said: “I am a poor scholar — what can I manage?” The Daoist said: “Good deeds and hidden merit are all created from the heart. Keep this heart always, and your merit will be measureless. Take humility alone: it costs not a single coin. Why then do you not examine yourself, instead of cursing the examiner?”
From this Zhang bowed his pride and held himself in check; he cultivated his good day after day and deepened his virtue day after day. In the year Dingyou (at Master Liaofan’s

years of age), he dreamed of coming to a tall house where he found a register of the examination list, with many lines left blank. He asked the people beside him, and they said: “This is the register for the present examination.” He asked: “Why are so many names missing?” They said: “Civil degrees are assessed once every three years in the underworld; only those who have accumulated virtue and are without fault receive a place. Those whom you see blank were originally due to pass, but were struck off because of newly committed light misdemeanors.” Then, pointing to one line, they said: “For the past three years you have been quite careful in your conduct; you may perhaps be added in this place. Take heed and cherish yourself.” In that examination he indeed passed in the hundred-and-fifth place.

From this we see that above one’s head, three feet high, there certainly are spirits and gods; and that to draw near good fortune and keep from evil is decisively in our own hands. We must so keep our heart and govern our conduct as not to offend Heaven and Earth, the spirits and gods, by the least jot; and we must humble ourselves and empty the heart, so that Heaven and Earth and the spirits and gods are always pitying us — only then is there a foundation for receiving blessing. Those whose spirit swells are certainly not vessels of far-reaching destiny, and even if they rise to fortune, it will give them no true enjoyment. Any man of a little sight would never bear to narrow his own measure and thereby push away his own blessing. Moreover, humility gives room in which to receive instruction and an endless store of good to take up, and is above all indispensable to one who is cultivating his task.

An ancient saying goes: “He who sets his heart upon fame and rank will surely attain fame and rank; he who sets his heart upon wealth and honor will surely attain wealth and honor.” A man’s having a purpose is like a tree’s having a root. Once this purpose is firmly set, you must keep every single thought humble and every single occasion an occasion of service, and of itself it will move Heaven and Earth — and then the making of blessing rests with me.

Those who today seek to pass the examination never had a true purpose to begin with — it is only a passing fancy: when the mood comes they seek, and when the mood fades they stop. Mencius said: “If the King’s love of music were great indeed, then his state would be near to its perfect order!” And so it is with me and rank in the examinations.
